extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, and policy-makers interested in peer review, scientific publishing, and bias in evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating scientific manuscripts (peer review) including which review criteria matter, mechanisms of reviewer bias, and policies/practices to reduce biased or unreliable assessments. Emphasis on retrospective manuscript review (scientific validity) and reviewer-author social connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific validity (PLOS ONE instruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: PLOS ONE instructs reviewers to evaluate manuscripts only on scientific validity — i.e., whether the work is properly done science — decoupling impact/novelty assessment from technical assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat validity as the primary, objective criterion. PLOS ONE’s mission is to publish work meeting high standards of scientific validity regardless of perceived novelty or impact. This reduces incentives for nepotistic review and encourages focusing reviewers on methodological correctness, clarity, and adherence to data policies. Note: even validity judgments show substantial disagreement (inter-rater reliability ~0.19 in this dataset).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / Novelty / Originality (subjective criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional journals instruct reviewers to judge 'significance', 'novelty', or 'originality' in addition to validity; these are interpretively flexible and inherently more uncertain than technical validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that these 'soft' criteria invite divergent interpretations across reviewers (e.g., humanists vs social scientists value different kinds of originality). Because they are judgments about uncertain future impact, they increase disagreement and favoritism. One mitigation is to separate technical (validity) from subjective (impact) evaluation or perform impact assessment post-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nepotism / particularistic bias (conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularistic considerations—anything tied to creators rather than the content (e.g., gender, race, institutional affiliation, personal connections)—constitute nepotism when reviewers favor closely connected authors on non-scientific grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies commonly recuse the most closely connected reviewers (e.g., advisors, co-authors) to limit nepotism. Nepotism is more likely in competitive settings; reducing competition and recusal can reduce nepotistic incentives. However, recusal of only the closest ties may not eliminate all bias because other mechanisms (subjective criteria, schools of thought) also cause favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schools of thought (substantive alignment bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communities of like-minded scholars ('schools of thought') share methodological, theoretical, and epistemological assumptions; reviewers from the same school tend to favor each other's work because it aligns with their substantive views, producing bias distinct from nepotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because schools-of-thought bias arises from substantive agreement, merely recusing close personal ties will not eliminate it. To mitigate, recruit reviewers from diverse scientific clusters and professional networks so that multiple substantive perspectives are represented in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and information asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Review contexts differ: prospective judgments (grants, promotions) often involve uncertainty and information asymmetry (reviewers may have private info), while retrospective manuscript review should reduce asymmetry since work is complete and described in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reviewers with topical expertise to minimize information asymmetry. In settings with strong asymmetry (e.g., grant panels), favoritism may reflect access to private information; in manuscript review, other mechanisms (schools of thought, subjective criteria) are more salient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability / agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review typically shows low inter-rater reliabilities (examples: ICC and kappa values commonly in the 0.10–0.40 range; PLOS ONE inter-rater reliability reported as 0.19), indicating frequent disagreement among reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure reliability (e.g., intra-class correlation, Cohen's kappa). Low reliability suggests evaluations diverge even on technical criteria and indicates limits of relying on single reviewers. Use multiple independent reviews, calibration procedures, or structured review forms to try to increase reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition intensity (effect on nepotism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher competition increases incentives for nepotistic or self-serving reviews; competitive environments are more likely to see reviewers favoring personal connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing competition (e.g., journals with high acceptance rates or post-publication impact assessment) should reduce nepotistic behavior. Consider structural reforms that lower zero-sum stakes when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection and network diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is chosen to review matters: reviewers embedded in diverse professional networks bring different perspectives and reduce the likelihood that a single school of thought dominates evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively recruit reviewers from varied co-authorship networks and epistemic communities to counteract homophily-driven bias. Diversity of reviewer schools increases the chance that substantive disagreements are represented and balanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-blind vs double-blind review
rubrics_metrics.description: Many journals use single-blind review (reviewers see authors' identities). The intuitive expectation that single-blind enables more relational bias is not strongly supported by consistent empirical evidence; studies are mixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider blinding (double-blind) as one tool, but be aware evidence of improvement is inconsistent and may be limited by unsuccessful blinding (reviewers guessing identities). Editors should weigh practical constraints and uncertain benefits when choosing blinding policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of technical (objective) vs subjective review components
rubrics_metrics.description: Collapsing technical and subjective criteria in a single overall judgment increases ambiguity and may conflate validity with impact; separating them can reduce bias tied to subjective judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design review forms and processes that explicitly separate assessments of methodological/technical validity from evaluations of novelty/impact. This can clarify what reviewers are being asked to judge and may reduce favoritism driven by subjective tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recusal policies (which relationships to exclude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard recusal practice excludes the most closely connected individuals (e.g., dissertation advisors, recent co-authors) from reviewing to avoid obvious conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement clear recusal rules for close professional relationships. Be mindful that recusal of only the closest ties may not address more diffuse biases (e.g., schools of thought) and that policies should be complemented by reviewer diversity and other safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training on conscious and non-conscious biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Training reviewers about bias (conscious and unconscious) is proposed as a potential mitigation for nepotism and other particularistic influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer reviewer training to raise awareness of bias sources and to instruct reviewers on focusing on appropriate criteria. Training alone may not eliminate structural sources of bias (like schools of thought) but can be part of a broader mitigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Score calibration and discussion effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Score-calibration talk and panel discussion influence intra- and inter-panel variability in ratings (score calibration can change how reviewers map judgments to scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calibration discussions, norming sessions, or structured scoring rubrics to reduce variability caused by differing internal scales among reviewers. Be careful: calibration dynamics can also introduce social influences that change independence of judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to journal policies (clear writing and data policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may require manuscripts to be clearly written and to adhere to specific data policies as part of assessment (PLOS ONE requires clear writing and adherence to its data policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure manuscripts meet stated journal requirements (clarity, data accessibility) since non-adherence can be grounds for unfavorable review or rejection even when scientific validity is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-suggested reviewers and suggested flagging
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors sometimes nominate suggested reviewers; this author nomination correlates with co-authorship proximity and may affect reviewer choice and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track whether a reviewer was suggested by authors (the dataset codes 'Suggested' = 1 if author nominated). Use policies that vet author-suggested reviewers for conflicts and balance suggested names with editor-selected reviewers to limit bias from author influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring reviewer-author relatedness (co-authorship distance) — methodological standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-authorship network distance (e.g., co-author = distance 1; co-author-of-co-author = distance 2; 3+) is used to measure reviewer-author proximity, but measured distances are subject to missing data and temporal measurement error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using co-authorship networks, be explicit about network construction limits (one-level-out, API maximums), recode long distances (4+) as 3+ to address upward bias, and account for co-authorship timestamps (some links may postdate the review). Consider how missing nodes/edges bias measured distances and interpret closeness measures cautiously.
